3. and repository requirements, access mechanisms and contractual arrangements through which legal and institutional obligations may be operationalised. Inter-layer connectors represent the potential interaction of these governance levels; they do not denote a measured hierarchy, fixed sequence or numerical relationship. The figure is an interpretive legal synthesis based on the 10 selected North American governance units. It is not a frequency distribution, a jurisdictional ranking or an empirical assessment of technical performance or post-transformation protection. The North American units were not included in Figure 2 of the main manuscript or analysed through the sovereign-jurisdiction regional protocol in Supplementary Table 2.3.

North America required an analytically distinct treatment because neurodata governance in the United States and Canada is distributed across federal, state or provincial, sector-specific, institutional and contractual frameworks. We therefore analysed 10 selected legally operative governance units, six in the United States and four in Canada, rather than treating each country as a single, internally uniform jurisdiction. These units were not included in the sovereign-jurisdiction distributions in Figure 2 of the main manuscript or synthesised through the common regional protocol in Supplementary Table 2. Instead, North America was examined separately as a distributed governance architecture (Supplementary Figure 1) and through the federated case studies presented later in this Supplementary Material.

Supplementary Figure 1 provides an interpretive synthesis of the relationships among four governance levels identified through the North American analysis. It does not suggest that the United States and Canada share a single legal framework or that the same rules apply uniformly across institutions, sectors,s or subnational jurisdictions. Rather, it illustrates why identifying the applicable governance environment requires consideration of the entity processing the neurodata, the purpose and context of processing, the location of the relevant actors, the applicable sectoral rules and the institutional or contractual conditions governing access and reuse.

At the federal level (Supplementary Figure 1a), the United States and Canada operate through distinct legal frameworks. In the United States, HIPAA regulates protected health information within the activities of covered entities and their business associates, while the Common Rule governs human-subjects research falling within its institutional and regulatory scope. Federal Trade Commission authority and associated rules may also be relevant in commercial or consumer-health contexts, including certain health applications and technologies not governed by HIPAA. In Canada, PIPEDA establishes federal private-sector requirements for the collection, use and disclosure of personal information in the course of commercial activities. These federal instruments provide important governance foundations, but none constitutes a comprehensive neurodata-specific regime, and their applicability depends on the entity, activity, data, and processing context concerned.

The subnational level (Supplementary Figure 1b) introduces further variation. In the United States, state laws such as the California Consumer Privacy Act and Washington's My Health My Data Act may impose additional obligations in consumer, commercial or non-HIPAA health-data contexts. In Canada, provincial private-sector, public-sector and personal-health-information laws may apply alongside or, in specified circumstances, instead of federal private-sector requirements. The applicable governance pathway must therefore be determined contextually rather than inferred from the country of origin or destination alone.

Institutional governance (Supplementary Figure 1c) provides a further operational layer. Institutional review boards or research ethics boards, privacy officers, data access committees, repositories and participating research organisations may translate applicable legal and ethical requirements into project-specific conditions governing collection, access, secondary use, repository deposit and onward sharing. Where legislation does not exhaustively determine these operational matters, institutional policies, access procedures and ethics requirements may specify additional controls. Variation among institutional arrangements may consequently affect the conditions under which a particular collaboration proceeds. The comparative legal study did not, however, systematically measure changes in institutional priorities or their effects on access and participation.

The technical and contractual level (Supplementary Figure 1d) includes information-security requirements, access controls, cloud and repository conditions, data-use agreements and other contractual mechanisms through which legal and institutional obligations may be implemented. These mechanisms can influence the practical feasibility of hosting, accessing and sharing neurodata, but their existence does not by itself establish equivalent technical performance or governance effectiveness. The coding examined the legal requirements for safeguards and contractual governance; it did not directly test technical systems or determine whether protection persists, weakens or changes after neurodata are transformed into derivatives, embeddings or model-associated artefacts.

3.

In synthesis, North American neurodata governance is best characterised as distributed and sectorally differentiated rather than governed through a single nationally harmonised framework. This distributed structure should not be equated with a complete absence of regulation: multiple legal and institutional controls may apply concurrently, but their applicability and interaction are pathway-specific. International collaboration with an institution in the United States or Canada may therefore require the concurrent evaluation of federal, subnational, sector-specific, institutional and contractual requirements.

This analysis supports the paper's finding that cross-border neurodata exchange depends on conditional interoperability rather than legal authorisation alone. It does not establish that the North American architecture is uniformly more or less protective than the sovereign-jurisdiction architectures examined elsewhere, nor does it demonstrate how protection changes throughout the complete data-to-model lifecycle. The proposed assessment of post-transformation functional exposure remains a normative and methodological extension of the comparative legal findings.

Qualitative and quantitative question-driven analytic protocol used for the regional comparative analysis

The regional comparative analysis constituted the second stage of the study's sequential legal-analytical design.

Whereas the jurisdiction-level protocol in Supplementary Table 1 generated standardised governance profiles, the regional stage synthesised the profiles of the 93 sovereign jurisdictions included from Africa, Europe, and Latin America and the Caribbean. The six-layer governance framework in Figure 1 of the main manuscript was used as a structured comparative framework rather than as a numerical scoring instrument. This enabled recurring regional patterns to be examined while retaining the legal context, qualifications and jurisdiction-specific reasoning underlying each categorical classification.

We began by reviewing the standardised coded responses and supporting legal narratives recorded in Supplementary Data 3. For each governance question, the categorical responses were summarised within the three regions to indicate how frequently particular legal or governance characteristics appeared among the sampled jurisdictions. These descriptive distributions were used to generate Figure 2 of the main manuscript. No weighting or numerical score was assigned to the individual governance indicators, and the resulting percentages are not inferential statistical estimates. They provide a visual summary of the standardised legal coding rather than an independent quantitative analysis.

The descriptive distributions were then interpreted by returning to the underlying jurisdictional profiles and supporting legal sources. The frequencies were used to identify questions requiring further comparative interpretation rather than being treated as findings in themselves. For each of the six governance layers, we considered the distribution of the coded categories together with the legal definitions, qualifications, exceptions, areas of ambiguity, and forms of missing or unavailable evidence recorded in the jurisdictional analyses. This process supported the identification of recurring patterns and areas of convergence or divergence without implying that jurisdictions assigned to the same broad category were doctrinally, institutionally, or operationally equivalent. Because the study did not conduct a longitudinal legal analysis, the synthesis does not claim to measure regulatory trends over time.

The regional analytical protocol used for this interpretive synthesis is presented in Supplementary Table 2. For each governance layer, the protocol identifies the evidence base, the comparative legal questions applied to that evidence and the form of regional insight sought. The resulting regional findings are summarised in Supplementary Table 3, with the supporting jurisdictional data and regional analyses provided in Supplementary Data 3.

The 10 North American governance units were not included in these regional frequency distributions or synthesised through the common protocol in Supplementary Table 2 because they were not analytically equivalent to the sovereign-jurisdiction units. North America was examined separately as a distributed governance architecture and through federated case studies of Canada and the United States. Where Supplementary Table 3 places the North American findings alongside the three sovereign-jurisdiction regional summaries, it does so for comparative overview purposes while preserving this distinct analytical basis.

Qualitative regional findings: Africa Layer 1. Definitions and conceptual scope

The country-level analyses showed that neurodata is not explicitly recognised as a distinct legal object in any of the African jurisdictions examined. Instead, it is consistently absorbed into existing legal categories, most commonly health data and, in some instances, biometric or mental data, allowing neurodata to benefit from the heightened protections afforded to sensitive personal information. The aggregated coding demonstrated a high degree of consistency across the region, with only isolated jurisdictions exhibiting fragmented or incomplete data protection frameworks.

Although this approach provides a baseline level of legal protection, it also obscures the distinctive characteristics of neurodata. Across the region, neurodata is primarily framed as informational or bodily data rather than as information directly implicating cognition, mental autonomy, or identity. Existing legal protections therefore focus on established data protection principles, including consent, confidentiality, security safeguards, and ethics oversight, while providing little recognition of risks associated with neural inference, behavioural prediction, cognitive manipulation, or mental privacy. Similarly, neurorights do not appear as enforceable legal rights and are discussed only indirectly through broader constitutional rights such as privacy, dignity, bodily integrity, and freedom of thought.

The regional analysis also identified substantial fragmentation across regulatory sectors. Neurodata receives its strongest protection within healthcare and biomedical research, whereas consumer, employment, and commercial settings rely largely on general data protection law without recognising the distinctive characteristics of neurotechnologies. Consequently, neurodata may move between sectors under markedly different governance standards. Collectively, these findings indicate that African jurisdictions provide procedural protection for neurodata while remaining conceptually unable to distinguish it from other forms of sensitive personal information, creating important regulatory gaps for emerging neurotechnologies.

Layer 2. Lawful bases and consent

The country-level coding demonstrated that African legal frameworks are formally centred on consent as the principal lawful basis for processing neurodata through its classification as sensitive or health-related information. However, the aggregated regional findings show that consent is rarely absolute. Most jurisdictions permit processing under a range of alternative lawful bases, including public interest, public health, scientific research, legal obligation, and institutional mandates, making consent an important but context-dependent mechanism rather than an enduring source of individual control.

The comparative analysis further showed that consent functions primarily as a procedural safeguard rather than as a substantive guarantee of autonomy. Although legal frameworks generally require consent to be informed, specific, and voluntary, few explicitly address the structural power imbalances experienced by patients, employees, research participants, or consumers. Scientific research occupies a particularly privileged position across the region, with ethics committee review functioning as the principal safeguard where consent is relaxed or waived. Responsibility for protecting participants therefore shifts from individuals to institutions, while oversight remains focused primarily on research design and regulatory compliance rather than on downstream uses of neurodata.

Commercial processing follows a similar pattern. Once neurodata has been lawfully collected, existing legal frameworks generally permit its subsequent use through contractual arrangements and other recognised lawful bases, while offering comparatively limited protection against profiling, behavioural influence, or commercial exploitation. The regional evidence therefore suggests that African governance is formally autonomy-oriented but operates predominantly through institutional and public-interest logics, with individual control becoming progressively weaker throughout the data lifecycle.

Layer 3. Cross-border transfers

The aggregated country-level findings showed that African jurisdictions generally regard cross-border transfers of neurodata as conditionally permissible rather than inherently prohibited. Most legal frameworks rely on broad adequacy requirements, regulatory approval, consent, or contractual safeguards to facilitate international data sharing while maintaining participation in global research collaborations and digital health initiatives. Formal adequacy determinations remain uncommon, with most jurisdictions instead adopting flexible mechanisms based on functional equivalence.

The regional comparison further revealed that African transfer regimes are designed primarily to enable international interoperability rather than to impose strict territorial controls. Transfer provisions are generally expressed in broad, principle-based terms and rely heavily on institutional discretion rather than detailed procedural mechanisms. Trust is placed principally in research institutions, data controllers, regulatory authorities, and contractual arrangements, while technical safeguards such as encryption play a secondary role. Although research-related transfers are frequently treated more permissive than commercial transfers, legal frameworks rarely distinguish between transfers to different geopolitical regions, leaving broader global inequalities in data governance largely unaddressed.

Taken together, these findings indicate that African cross-border governance is best characterised as conditionally permissive and institution-centred. Existing transfer mechanisms facilitate international collaboration but do not specifically address the distinctive risks associated with exporting neurodata, including heightened risks to mental privacy, cognitive autonomy, and downstream inferential uses.

National frameworks operate alongside continental initiatives, including the AU Data Policy Framework (2022), the Malabo Convention, which entered into force in 2023, and the AU Continental AI Strategy (2024). These instruments have different legal effects: treaty obligations depend on participation and domestic implementation, while the policy frameworks guide regional convergence rather than independently authorising transfers. Their relevance to pathway assessment and contractual safeguards must therefore be evaluated alongside applicable national law.

Layer 4. Safeguards and oversight

The regional coding showed that most African jurisdictions provide formal safeguards for sensitive personal information through data protection legislation, ethics review processes, and oversight by data protection authorities or research ethics committees. Individual rights of access, correction, withdrawal of consent, and complaint are widely recognised in principle, although their practical implementation varies considerably across jurisdictions. Oversight mechanisms are strongest within health research and clinical settings, where established institutional governance structures already exist.

Despite these procedural safeguards, the comparative analysis demonstrated important differences in institutional capacity and effectiveness. Oversight bodies often operate with limited resources, while governance arrangements remain focused on conventional data protection obligations rather than the distinctive challenges posed by neurotechnologies. Repository governance, downstream access decisions, and secondary uses of neurodata receive comparatively little explicit regulatory attention. As a result, legal safeguards tend to concentrate on compliance at the point of collection rather than on continuous governance throughout the neurodata lifecycle.

The regional evidence therefore suggests that African governance relies predominantly on preventive procedural safeguards while offering comparatively limited mechanisms for monitoring or controlling subsequent uses of neurodata. Protection is strongest within established research and healthcare environments but becomes considerably weaker as neurodata moves into commercial or cross-sectoral contexts.

Layer 5. Enforcement and remedies

The country-level analyses indicated that African jurisdictions generally provide formal mechanisms for enforcement through data protection authorities, administrative sanctions, and judicial remedies. Liability for unlawful processing is usually allocated to data controllers or responsible institutions, while legislation commonly provides individuals with rights to lodge complaints and seek legal remedies for violations of data protection law. Nevertheless, practical enforcement capacity varies substantially across jurisdictions, reflecting differences in institutional maturity, regulatory resources, and implementation experience.

The comparative analysis also showed that enforcement remains largely oriented towards conventional data protection violations rather than harms arising from neurotechnologies. Few jurisdictions have practical experience addressing issues such as cognitive manipulation, neural inference, behavioural prediction, or secondary commercial uses of neurodata. Consequently, although legal remedies formally exist, their effectiveness in responding to emerging neurotechnology-related harms remains uncertain. Individuals often bear a significant burden in identifying violations and pursuing enforcement, particularly where downstream processing occurs across institutional or jurisdictional boundaries.

Collectively, these findings suggest that African legal frameworks establish credible procedural enforcement mechanisms but remain insufficiently equipped to address the novel harms associated with neurodata. Existing remedies therefore provide an important foundation for accountability while leaving significant gaps in the practical protection of mental privacy and cognitive autonomy.

Layer 6. Contractual governance

The regional coding demonstrated that contractual arrangements play an increasingly important role in the governance of neurodata once it moves beyond healthcare and publicly funded research. Although public law provides the overarching regulatory framework, contractual agreements frequently determine the practical conditions governing access, sharing, processing, and secondary use of neurodata across commercial and research environments. Data subjects typically participate through standardised consent forms or contractual terms rather than through individually negotiated arrangements.

The comparative analysis indicated that contracts generally implement existing public law obligations rather than replace them entirely. Nevertheless, contractual governance often operates within significant power asymmetries, particularly where individuals engage with commercial neurotechnology providers or digital health platforms. Existing legal frameworks provide relatively little scrutiny of contractual fairness or the broader implications of private ordering for mental privacy and cognitive autonomy. As neurodata increasingly circulates through transnational research collaborations and commercial partnerships, contractual governance assumes a progressively more significant role in determining practical rights and responsibilities.

Viewed together, these findings indicate that African neurodata governance remains predominantly grounded in public law but increasingly depends upon hybrid governance arrangements in which contractual mechanisms supplement statutory protections. This growing reliance on private ordering highlights the need for stronger safeguards to ensure that contractual governance remains consistent with broader principles of accountability, transparency, and protection of fundamental rights.

Qualitative regional findings: Europe

"Europe" denotes a geographical grouping of 22 EU Member States, the United Kingdom, and Switzerland, each coded separately. Regional similarities do not imply legal equivalence: the UK GDPR and Data Protection Act 2018 constitute a distinct domestic framework, and EU legislation is not treated as automatically applicable to the UK.

3.

Layer 1. Definitions and conceptual scope

The country-level analyses demonstrated that none of the European jurisdictions examined explicitly recognise neurodata as a distinct legal category. Instead, neurodata is consistently governed through existing legal classifications, principally as health data and, depending on the context, as biometric or other forms of special category personal data. The aggregated coding revealed remarkable consistency across the region, reflecting EU GDPR harmonisation among the sampled EU Member States and similarities with the separately coded UK and Swiss frameworks. As a result, neurodata benefits from the highest level of protection available under European data protection law despite the absence of explicit legal recognition.

The regional analysis nevertheless showed that this regulatory model protects neurodata procedurally while obscuring its conceptual distinctiveness. Neurodata is predominantly framed as informational data, with only limited recognition of its bodily origins and little acknowledgement of its intimate relationship to cognition, identity, or mental autonomy. Existing safeguards therefore address neurodata insofar as it resembles health or biometric information, rather than because of its unique capacity to reveal or infer mental states, emotions, intentions, or behavioural traits. Likewise, neurorights remain absent from binding legislation, appearing primarily within policy initiatives, ethical guidance, and academic discourse, while existing constitutional protections provide only indirect safeguards through rights such as privacy, dignity, and freedom of thought.

The comparative analysis also identified important differences across regulatory sectors. Healthcare and scientific research benefit from comprehensive governance through data protection law, medical regulation, and research ethics oversight, whereas consumer neurotechnology, employment, and commercial applications remain comparatively fragmented. Consequently, Europe governs neurodata through a mature procedural framework but continues to regulate it as a derivative form of sensitive personal information rather than as a distinct legal object. These findings suggest that European governance is characterised by implicit legal exceptionalism, providing strong baseline protections while leaving important neurotechnology-specific risks insufficiently addressed.

Layer 2. Lawful bases and consent

The aggregated country-level findings showed that Europe adopts a plural model of lawful processing in which consent remains important but is no longer the principal source of legal authority for neurodata processing. Across the jurisdictions analysed, scientific research, healthcare, and public-interest functions frequently rely on statutory research derogations and other lawful bases provided by the EU GDPR, UK and Swiss data protection legislation (as applicable), and equivalent national legislation. Consent therefore operates as one lawful basis among several. Whether consent is required, and the role it plays, depends on the nature of the processing and applicable national law.

The comparative analysis demonstrated that this governance model prioritises institutional accountability over continuous individual control. Although consent remains a central expression of personal autonomy, particularly in commercial settings, European legal frameworks explicitly recognise situations in which consent cannot realistically function as a reliable safeguard, including employment relationships and many forms of scientific research. In these contexts, ethics committee review, data minimisation, pseudonymisation, proportionality, and institutional oversight replace individual authorisation as the principal mechanisms of protection. Consequently, responsibility for safeguarding neurodata shifts from data subjects to research institutions and regulatory authorities.

Commercial uses follow a comparable logic. Once neurodata has been lawfully collected, existing legal frameworks generally facilitate secondary processing through contractual arrangements, legitimate interests, and other recognised lawful bases, while providing comparatively limited attention to consumer vulnerability, behavioural manipulation, or inferential harms. Collectively, these findings indicate that Europe has developed a governance model centred primarily on public interest and institutional responsibility. Individual autonomy remains an important legal principle, but it operates 3.

within a broader framework that prioritises socially beneficial uses of neurodata through structured institutional governance.

Layer 3. Cross-border transfers

The country-level coding demonstrated that European jurisdictions treat cross-border transfers of neurodata as conditionally permissible rather than inherently prohibited. International transfers are regarded as an integral component of scientific collaboration, healthcare, and digital innovation, provided that equivalent levels of legal protection accompany the data beyond national borders. Unlike the more flexible transfer regimes identified elsewhere, European governance relies upon detailed adequacy mechanisms, contractual safeguards, and supplementary measures designed to preserve fundamental rights throughout international data flows.

The comparative analysis further showed that European transfer rules are built upon a sophisticated legal infrastructure centred on accountability and risk management. Trust is placed not only in institutions and contractual arrangements but also in formal adequacy decisions and detailed regulatory mechanisms that assess the legal protections available within recipient jurisdictions. Research transfers generally benefit from more flexible arrangements than commercial transfers, reflecting the continued importance of scientific collaboration while maintaining a strong commitment to fundamental rights protection. At the same time, governance remains largely data-centred rather than neurodata-specific, with transfer mechanisms applying equally to other forms of special category personal data.

Viewed together, these findings indicate that Europe has developed the most comprehensive cross-border governance framework among the regions examined. The legal emphasis on accountability, adequacy, and enforceable safeguards provides robust protection for international data sharing, although existing mechanisms continue to address neurodata primarily through general data protection principles rather than through recognition of its distinctive cognitive and inferential characteristics.

Layer 4. Safeguards and oversight

The regional analysis demonstrated that Europe possesses a mature system of institutional safeguards supporting the governance of neurodata. Across the jurisdictions analysed, data protection authorities, research ethics committees, medical regulatory bodies, and judicial oversight collectively provide multiple layers of accountability throughout the data lifecycle. Individual rights of access, rectification, objection, erasure, and withdrawal of consent are widely recognised and supported by relatively well-developed institutional infrastructures.

Despite these strengths, the comparative analysis identified limitations in the scope of existing safeguards. Oversight mechanisms remain primarily oriented towards ensuring compliance with established data protection obligations rather than addressing the distinctive challenges presented by neurotechnologies. Ethics committees continue to function principally as gateways for research approval, while ongoing oversight of secondary uses, downstream data sharing, algorithmic inference, and commercial reuse remains comparatively limited. As neurodata increasingly moves beyond healthcare and academic research into consumer and workplace environments, existing governance mechanisms become less coherent and more fragmented.

The regional findings therefore suggest that Europe has developed a predominantly preventive governance model built upon strong institutional oversight and enforceable legal rights. Nevertheless, these safeguards continue to focus on conventional data protection risks and have yet to evolve fully towards the governance challenges associated with mental privacy, cognitive autonomy, and emerging neurotechnologies.

The Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 illustrates the UK framework's distinct legislative development. Section 80 provides for a more permissive approach to solely automated decisions producing legal or similarly significant effects where special-category data are not involved, subject to applicable lawful-processing requirements and safeguards for 3.

information, representations, human intervention and contestation. Stricter restrictions remain where such decisions involve special-category data, including neurodata classified as health data. Although enacted before the 31 December 2025 cutoff, the substantive reform commenced on 5 February 2026. Its subsequent operation is noted here for context and is not treated as law operative at the coding cutoff.

Layer 5. Enforcement and remedies

The country-level analyses showed that European jurisdictions provide well-established mechanisms for enforcement through independent supervisory authorities, administrative sanctions, judicial review, and individual legal remedies. Responsibility for compliance is clearly allocated to data controllers and processors, while within the EU, the GDPR provides a comprehensive framework for investigations, corrective measures, and financial penalties. Compared with the other regions examined, Europe exhibits the most mature institutional capacity for enforcing data protection obligations.

The comparative analysis nevertheless demonstrated that enforcement remains focused primarily on conventional infringements of data protection law. Existing mechanisms are well equipped to address unlawful processing, inadequate security, or failures to comply with procedural requirements, but considerably less developed in relation to emerging neurotechnology-specific harms such as cognitive profiling, behavioural manipulation, emotional inference, or downstream algorithmic decision-making. Consequently, although European legal frameworks provide highly effective procedural remedies, they remain less capable of addressing harms that arise from the unique characteristics of neurodata itself.

Collectively, these findings indicate that Europe has established a credible and well-resourced enforcement architecture capable of supporting strong regulatory compliance. However, the evolution of neurotechnologies is likely to require corresponding development of enforcement frameworks capable of responding to harms that extend beyond traditional conceptions of personal data protection.

Layer 6. Contractual governance

The regional coding demonstrated that contractual governance plays an important complementary role within the broader European regulatory framework. Public law continues to establish the principal obligations governing neurodata processing, while contractual arrangements operationalise these requirements across research collaborations, healthcare systems, cloud service providers, and commercial technology platforms. Contracts therefore function primarily as instruments implementing statutory obligations rather than replacing public regulation.

The comparative analysis nevertheless showed that contractual governance becomes increasingly influential once neurodata enters commercial environments. Consumer neurotechnology frequently relies on standardised contractual terms, while secondary processing, data sharing, and commercial analytics are often facilitated through private agreements operating within the limits established by the applicable data-protection regime. Although European law provides stronger safeguards against unfair contractual practices than many other jurisdictions, significant information asymmetries and unequal bargaining power continue to characterise many commercial relationships involving neurodata. Existing legal frameworks therefore offer comparatively limited scrutiny of how contractual arrangements may facilitate downstream behavioural profiling or commercial exploitation.

Taken together, these findings indicate that European governance remains predominantly grounded in public law but increasingly incorporates hybrid governance arrangements in which contractual mechanisms facilitate the practical implementation of statutory obligations. As neurotechnologies continue to expand into consumer and commercial domains, the relationship between public regulation and private ordering is likely to become an increasingly significant feature of European neurodata governance.

EHDS: scope and prospective implementation

The EU European Health Data Space Regulation (Regulation (EU) 2025/327) is relevant to prospective implementation of the toolkit. Applicability must be assessed against the relevant electronic-health-data category, health data holder, proposed purpose, territorial scope and application date; it should not be inferred solely from the neural origin of the data or the assigned functional-exposure tier. The assessment should distinguish statutory access under an EHDS data permit, requests for anonymised statistical results, and access through other lawful arrangements. For an applicable EHDS pathway, the decision record should identify the authorising body, permitted processing, authorised users, processing environment and release conditions. Access involving the United Kingdom, Switzerland, or other non-EU jurisdictions requires a separate assessment of the applicable access and international-transfer conditions. These prospective implementation considerations must be distinguished from the compatibility findings for the study cutoff.

Qualitative regional findings: Latin America and the Caribbean Layer 1. Definitions and conceptual scope

The country-level analyses revealed a heterogeneous regulatory landscape across Latin America and the Caribbean. Most jurisdictions do not explicitly recognise neurodata as a distinct legal object and instead regulate it indirectly through existing categories of health, biometric, mental, or other forms of sensitive personal data. The aggregated coding nevertheless identified important emerging exceptions. Chile has incorporated protections relating to neurotechnologies through constitutional reform, while Peru has explicitly recognised neurodata within its data protection legislation. Several other jurisdictions, including Brazil, Argentina, Mexico, and Uruguay, are actively considering legislative reforms, illustrating a region in transition rather than one characterised by regulatory uniformity.

The comparative analysis demonstrated that existing legal classifications provide important procedural safeguards but do not adequately capture the distinctive characteristics of neurodata. Although neurodata generally benefits from the highest level of protection afforded to sensitive personal information, these frameworks were developed to regulate conventional health or personal data rather than information capable of revealing cognitive processes, emotional states, behavioural traits, or neural activity. Consequently, neurodata remains conceptually subsumed within broader legal categories, limiting the ability of existing frameworks to address emerging challenges associated with mental privacy, cognitive autonomy, or neurotechnology-specific harms. Explicit neurorights remain the exception rather than the norm, with only limited legislative recognition across the region.

The regional comparison also highlighted substantial sectoral fragmentation. Healthcare and scientific research generally provide stronger governance through ethics review and health regulation, whereas consumer, employment, and commercial contexts rely predominantly on general data protection legislation. Viewed together, these findings indicate that Latin America and the Caribbean currently occupy a transitional position between conventional data protection governance and the emergence of neurotechnology-specific legal regulation.

Layer 2. Lawful bases and consent

The aggregated country-level coding demonstrated that consent remains the dominant lawful basis for processing neurodata across Latin America and the Caribbean. Unlike Europe, where research and public-interest exceptions frequently replace consent, most jurisdictions continue to place individual authorisation at the centre of their data protection frameworks. The regional summaries showed that consent is generally required before processing sensitive personal information, with only limited exceptions for scientific research, public interest, or other specifically authorised circumstances.

The comparative analysis further indicated that consent functions primarily as a substantive safeguard of individual autonomy rather than merely a procedural formality. Most jurisdictions explicitly recognise informed consent as the principal mechanism legitimising data processing and acknowledge the need to protect individuals in situations involving structural vulnerability, including healthcare, research, and employment. Scientific research nevertheless enjoys privileged legal treatment throughout much of the region. Where consent requirements are relaxed, ethics committee review, anonymisation, confidentiality obligations, and other institutional safeguards generally replace direct individual authorisation, reflecting an attempt to balance scientific advancement with participant protection.

Commercial processing follows a somewhat different trajectory. Neurodata may enter commercial contexts through contractual consent and other lawful mechanisms, although some jurisdictions impose stricter limitations on the commercialisation of sensitive personal information than those observed in other regions. Collectively, these findings suggest that Latin American and Caribbean governance remains predominantly autonomy-centred, with consent functioning as the principal organising principle while institutional safeguards support specific public-interest activities such as scientific research.

Layer 3. Cross-border transfers

The country-level analyses demonstrated considerable variation in approaches to cross-border transfers across the region. Most jurisdictions permit international transfers subject to specified legal conditions, while a smaller number rely on formal adequacy mechanisms or impose stricter limitations on outbound data flows. Unlike Europe, no single regional model governs international transfers, resulting in a diverse regulatory landscape that reflects differing levels of institutional development and legislative maturity.

The comparative analysis showed that existing transfer frameworks generally rely on broad legal principles rather than highly prescriptive procedural mechanisms. Trust is placed in institutional safeguards, contractual arrangements, technical security measures, and regulatory approval processes rather than in comprehensive regional adequacy systems. Scientific research frequently benefits from more flexible transfer arrangements than commercial activities, whereas commercial transfers remain subject primarily to consent and general data protection requirements. At the same time, important geopolitical asymmetries remain evident, with several jurisdictions continuing to structure international transfers around relationships with more established data protection systems outside the region rather than facilitating regional interoperability.

These findings suggest that cross-border governance within Latin America and the Caribbean is characterised by conditional openness combined with considerable institutional diversity. Existing legal frameworks generally facilitate international collaboration while providing comparatively limited neurodata-specific safeguards for international transfers, leaving governance dependent upon broader personal data protection principles.

Layer 4. Safeguards and oversight

The regional coding demonstrated that most jurisdictions provide formal oversight through data protection authorities, research ethics committees, judicial remedies, and constitutional mechanisms designed to protect individual rights. Rights of access, correction, deletion, and withdrawal of consent are widely recognised in legislation, although their practical implementation varies according to institutional capacity and national regulatory development. Countries with more mature data protection authorities generally provide stronger oversight than jurisdictions where regulatory institutions remain comparatively underdeveloped.

The comparative analysis nevertheless revealed important differences in the effectiveness of these safeguards. While oversight institutions frequently possess formal legal authority, practical implementation often depends upon available resources, administrative capacity, and broader institutional development. Existing governance mechanisms focus primarily on conventional data protection obligations rather than on the distinctive challenges presented by 3.

neurotechnologies, with relatively little explicit attention given to downstream processing, secondary uses, or algorithmic inference. Repository governance likewise remains largely institution-driven through research organisations and ethics committees.

Taken together, these findings indicate that the region has established a broadly preventive governance framework based upon recognised individual rights and institutional oversight. However, practical implementation remains uneven, and existing safeguards continue to address neurodata primarily through conventional data protection mechanisms rather than through dedicated neurotechnology governance.

Layer 5. Enforcement and remedies

The country-level analyses showed that most jurisdictions provide formal mechanisms for enforcement through administrative sanctions, judicial review, constitutional remedies, and oversight by national data protection authorities where these exist. Legal frameworks generally recognise individual rights to challenge unlawful processing and seek corrective action, although the availability and effectiveness of these mechanisms differ substantially across the region.

Countries with longer-established data protection systems generally demonstrate stronger enforcement capacity than jurisdictions where regulatory institutions remain comparatively recent or fragmented.

The comparative analysis also demonstrated that enforcement remains directed primarily towards traditional violations of data protection law rather than harms arising specifically from neurotechnologies. Existing remedies provide important mechanisms for addressing unlawful processing, failures to comply with consent requirements, or security breaches, but comparatively little regulatory experience exists in responding to cognitive profiling, behavioural manipulation, neural inference, or other neurotechnology-specific risks. Consequently, the effectiveness of current enforcement frameworks will depend upon their capacity to adapt as neurotechnologies become more widely deployed across healthcare, research, and commercial sectors.

Collectively, these findings suggest that enforcement frameworks across Latin America and the Caribbean provide an important foundation for accountability but remain at different stages of institutional maturity. While existing remedies are generally capable of supporting conventional data protection governance, further development may be required to address the distinctive legal challenges associated with neurodata.

Layer 6. Contractual governance

The regional coding demonstrated that contractual arrangements play an increasingly important role in governing neurodata across both research and commercial environments. Public law establishes the principal legal framework for processing sensitive personal information, while contracts operationalise these obligations through research collaborations, institutional agreements, cloud services, and commercial technology platforms. Individual participation is typically secured through consent incorporated within contractual arrangements, reflecting the central role of autonomy within regional data protection law.

The comparative analysis nevertheless showed that contractual governance assumes increasing significance as neurodata moves beyond healthcare and publicly funded research into private-sector applications. Although contractual freedom remains widely accepted, several jurisdictions impose additional limitations on the commercial use of sensitive personal information, reflecting a greater emphasis on protecting individual rights than on facilitating unrestricted commercial exploitation. At the same time, considerable variation exists across the region regarding institutional oversight, contractual safeguards, and regulatory scrutiny of downstream commercial uses. As neurotechnology markets continue to expand, contractual governance is likely to become an increasingly important mechanism through which legal protections are implemented in practice.

3.

Viewed together, these findings indicate that Latin America and the Caribbean continue to rely primarily on statutory data protection frameworks grounded in consent, while contractual governance increasingly complements public regulation in facilitating research, innovation, and commercial data sharing. The region's evolving legislative reforms suggest that contractual governance will likely develop alongside emerging neurotechnology-specific legal frameworks rather than independently of them.

Federated jurisdictional case studies: Canada and the United States

Unlike the regional comparative analyses presented above, Canada and the United States were examined as federated governance systems rather than as collections of sovereign jurisdictions. Consequently, the unit of comparison differs from that used for Africa, Europe, and Latin America and the Caribbean. Rather than comparing independent national legal systems within a geographic region, these analyses examined how neurodata governance is distributed across multiple constitutional levels within a single federated legal system.

The purpose of these case studies was to investigate how federal legislation interacts with selected provincial or state laws to create an overall governance framework for neurodata. In Canada, the analysis compared the federal Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) with selected provincial privacy and health information legislation from Québec, Ontario, and British Columbia. In the United States, the analysis examined the interaction between federal sector-specific frameworks, including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the Common Rule, and selected state privacy laws representing both established and emerging approaches to neurodata governance, including California, Colorado, Washington, and Kentucky.

The same six-layer governance ontology and standardised coding protocol described in 'Governance-level qualitative legal analysis and structured comparative coding' were applied throughout these analyses. However, unlike the regional findings, which identify patterns across sovereign jurisdictions, these case studies explore the interaction between different constitutional levels of governance within federated legal systems. The findings therefore focus on the degree of harmonisation or fragmentation between federal and subnational regulation, the allocation of regulatory authority, and the resulting governance architecture for neurodata.

These federated jurisdictional case studies complement the regional analyses by illustrating how constitutional structure influences neurodata governance. Together, they provide additional comparative insight into the ways in which governance frameworks evolve through both horizontal variation between countries and vertical variation across different levels of government within a single jurisdiction.

United States

The United States exhibits the most constitutionally fragmented governance framework among the jurisdictions examined in this study. Unlike the regional analyses presented above, which compare sovereign national legal systems, this case study examines how neurodata governance is distributed across multiple constitutional levels within a federated legal system. The analysis compares the federal regulatory framework-including the Health Insurance Portability and Accountability Act (HIPAA) and the Common Rule-with selected state privacy statutes representing both established and emerging approaches to neurodata governance, including California, Colorado, Washington, and Kentucky. Together, these legal instruments illustrate how federal sector-specific regulation increasingly operates alongside state-level legislative innovation to shape the governance of neurodata.

Layer 1. Definitions and conceptual scope

Comparison across the federal and state legal frameworks demonstrated substantial conceptual fragmentation in the governance of neurodata. Federal legislation, including HIPAA and the Common Rule, does not explicitly recognise neurodata as a distinct legal category, instead regulating it indirectly through established concepts such as protected health information and research data. In contrast, California and Colorado have introduced explicit statutory definitions of neural data within their consumer privacy legislation, while Washington and Kentucky continue to regulate neurodata through broader categories of health, biometric, or sensitive personal information. This diversity represents the greatest degree of conceptual variation observed across all jurisdictions included in the study.

The comparative analysis demonstrated that this fragmented legal architecture produces uneven recognition of neurodata's distinctive characteristics. Although explicit state definitions acknowledge neurodata as information generated through nervous system activity, these provisions continue to embed neural data within existing privacy frameworks rather than establishing sui generis legal protection. Federal law remains predominantly oriented towards health and research contexts, while state consumer privacy laws increasingly recognise broader commercial applications of neurotechnology. Consequently, neurodata receives different levels of legal recognition depending on where it is collected, who processes it, and which statutory framework applies.

Collectively, these findings indicate that the United States has developed a decentralised governance model in which innovation occurs primarily through state legislation rather than comprehensive federal reform. State privacy laws increasingly supplement federal regulation, but the absence of a unified conceptual framework continues to produce significant variability in legal protection across sectors and jurisdictions.

Layer 2. Lawful bases and consent

Comparison across the federal and state frameworks demonstrated that authority to process neurodata varies considerably according to regulatory context. Unlike jurisdictions operating under comprehensive data protection legislation, the United States does not employ a unified system of lawful bases for processing personal information. Instead, federal healthcare regulation relies primarily on statutory authorisation, research governance emphasises informed consent and institutional review, while state privacy laws increasingly require consent or opt-in mechanisms for processing sensitive or neural data.

The comparative analysis further revealed that consent performs markedly different functions across constitutional levels. Under the Common Rule, informed consent remains a substantive safeguard supporting participant autonomy in research, whereas HIPAA permits numerous routine healthcare uses without individual authorisation. State privacy legislation increasingly strengthens consent requirements in consumer contexts through opt-in or opt-out mechanisms, particularly for sensitive personal information. Despite these developments, recognition of structural power imbalances remains comparatively limited, particularly within employment settings where comprehensive privacy protections are largely absent.

Scientific research continues to receive privileged legal treatment across both federal and state frameworks. Where consent requirements are relaxed, institutional review boards, data minimisation, de-identification, and research exemptions provide alternative safeguards. Overall, the federated analysis indicates that U.S. governance combines multiple models of authorisation within a highly sector-specific legal architecture, reflecting the broader constitutional fragmentation that characterises American privacy law.

Layer 3. Cross-border transfers

US cross-border neurodata governance combines sector-specific duties, institutional, and contractual controls, and targeted federal restrictions. For an EU-to-US research pathway, the exporter must identify an applicable GDPR transfer 3.

mechanism and the EU-US Data Privacy Framework adequacy decision applies to eligible transfers to participating US organisations, while other recipients may still require safeguards such as standard contractual clauses (SCCs). The receiving institution's participation and the scope of coverage must be verified, US location alone does not establish eligibility. For an Africa-to-US pathway, applicable origin-country requirements must likewise be assessed separately from US recipient obligations. In either case, transfer permission does not itself authorise repository publication, onward sharing, or model release.

On the US side, the Department of Justice's Data Security Program under 28 CFR Part 202, effective from 8 April 2025, prohibits or restricts specified transactions involving US government-related data or bulk US sensitive personal data and countries of concern or covered persons. Relevant categories include personal health, biometric, and human genomic or other human 'omic data. Applicability depends on the data, transaction, parties, thresholds and available exemptions; the programme is not a general prohibition on international research collaboration. Proposed onward access must therefore be screened alongside applicable privacy, research, repository and contractual requirements.

The comparative analysis demonstrated that international transfers occupy a comparatively limited role within U.S. neurodata governance. Unlike jurisdictions that establish dedicated legal frameworks governing international transfers of personal data, neither federal healthcare legislation nor the state privacy laws examined provide a comprehensive regulatory architecture specifically addressing cross-border transfers of neurodata. Instead, international data sharing is governed largely through general contractual arrangements, institutional accountability, and sector-specific legal obligations.

This absence of dedicated transfer regulation reflects the broader structure of U.S. privacy law, which generally emphasises organisational accountability rather than restrictions on international data movement. Consequently, legal protection depends primarily upon the obligations imposed on individual organisations rather than on assessments of destination jurisdictions or formal adequacy mechanisms. Existing governance therefore provides relatively limited recognition of the particular risks associated with transferring neurodata across national boundaries.

Taken together, these findings indicate that cross-border governance remains underdeveloped within the U.S. regulatory framework. Rather than constituting a distinct area of neurodata governance, international transfers are largely incorporated into broader organisational compliance and contractual governance mechanisms.

Layer 4. Safeguards and oversight

Comparison across federal and state institutions demonstrated that oversight within the United States is similarly fragmented. Federal agencies, including the Department of Health and Human Services Office for Civil Rights and the Office for Human Research Protections, exercise oversight within healthcare and federally regulated research, while state attorneys general and specialised agencies such as the California Privacy Protection Agency supervise compliance with state privacy legislation. Unlike many other jurisdictions examined, however, the United States lacks a single independent national data protection authority responsible for overseeing personal data governance across sectors.

State privacy law also increasingly employs ex ante risk assessment as a preventive safeguard. The Colorado Privacy Act requires covered controllers to conduct data protection assessments before processing sensitive data and undertaking other processing activities presenting heightened risks to consumers. California had, by the study cutoff, finalized CCPA risk-assessment regulations requiring covered businesses to conduct and document risk assessments before specified processing presenting significant privacy risk, including processing sensitive personal information, those regulations took effect on 1 January 2026. Kentucky had likewise enacted a requirement for documented data protection impact assessments in relation to sensitive-data processing and other specified high-risk activities, effective from 2026. These provisions do not establish a uniform US impact assessment regime, but they demonstrate that state privacy governance increasingly includes prospective and documented assessment duties alongside consent, transparency and enforcement requirements.

3.

The comparative analysis further showed that safeguards are distributed across multiple regulatory institutions rather than integrated within a unified governance framework. Institutional review boards continue to provide important oversight within research, while federal healthcare regulators focus on covered entities and state privacy authorities oversee consumer protection obligations. This institutional diversity provides multiple avenues of accountability but also contributes to regulatory inconsistency and uneven protection outside traditional healthcare and research environments.

Collectively, these findings indicate that the United States relies upon decentralised institutional oversight reflecting its broader constitutional structure. Oversight mechanisms remain strongest within healthcare and federally funded research, while governance of consumer neurotechnology depends increasingly upon state-level regulatory capacity.

Layer 5. Enforcement and remedies

The federated analysis demonstrated that enforcement mechanisms are well established but highly decentralised. Federal agencies possess significant investigative and enforcement powers within their respective areas of competence, while state attorneys general exercise primary responsibility for enforcing state privacy legislation. Several state laws additionally provide limited private rights of action, although the availability of individual remedies varies considerably across jurisdictions.

The comparative analysis revealed that enforcement capacity differs substantially between constitutional levels. HIPAA violations may result in significant civil penalties and corrective action plans, while research oversight is enforced primarily through institutional compliance mechanisms. State privacy legislation increasingly supplements these mechanisms through administrative enforcement and, in some jurisdictions, private litigation. Nevertheless, enforcement remains directed primarily towards conventional privacy violations rather than harms uniquely associated with neurotechnology, such as cognitive inference, behavioural manipulation, or mental privacy intrusions.

Overall, the United States exhibits a robust but fragmented enforcement architecture in which responsibility is distributed among multiple federal and state authorities. Although these mechanisms provide meaningful accountability within existing legal frameworks, their effectiveness depends heavily upon the regulatory context in which neurodata is generated and processed.

Layer 6. Contractual governance

The comparative analysis found relatively limited statutory guidance concerning contractual governance of neurodata across both federal and state legal frameworks. Public law establishes the principal obligations governing healthcare, research, and consumer privacy, while contractual arrangements largely operate as implementation mechanisms through data use agreements, commercial service contracts, research collaborations, and organisational privacy policies. Existing legislation provides comparatively little direct regulation of contractual relationships governing downstream uses of neurodata.

As neurotechnology increasingly expands beyond traditional healthcare environments, contractual governance is likely to assume greater practical significance. Commercial entities frequently rely upon contractual terms and privacy notices to regulate data sharing, secondary processing, and interactions with third-party service providers. In the absence of comprehensive federal privacy legislation, these private ordering mechanisms increasingly shape how neurodata is collected, shared, and commercialised across consumer markets.

Taken together, these findings indicate that contractual governance currently complements rather than replaces statutory regulation. However, the continuing expansion of consumer neurotechnology suggests that private ordering may become an increasingly influential component of U.S. neurodata governance unless accompanied by broader legislative harmonisation across federal and state jurisdictions.

Canada

Canada presents a constitutionally decentralised yet comparatively coherent governance framework for neurodata. Unlike the regional analyses presented above, which compare sovereign national legal systems, this case study examines how neurodata governance is distributed across multiple constitutional levels within a federated legal system. The analysis compares the federal Personal Information Protection and Electronic Documents Act (PIPEDA) with selected provincial privacy and health information legislation from Québec, Ontario, and British Columbia. Together, these legislative frameworks illustrate how federal and provincial laws interact to create an integrated, although decentralised, system of neurodata governance.

Layer 1. Definitions and conceptual scope

Comparison across the federal and provincial legal frameworks demonstrated a high degree of conceptual consistency in the legal treatment of neurodata. Neither PIPEDA nor the provincial statutes examined explicitly recognise neurodata as a distinct legal category. Instead, neurodata is absorbed into existing legal concepts, including personal information, personal health information, and sensitive personal information, depending upon the jurisdiction and regulatory context.

The federal PIPEDA and the provincial law of Québec provide recognition of informational sensitivity through treatment of sensitive personal information, while Ontario's Personal Health Information Protection Act (PHIPA) principally regulates neurodata through a health information framework.

The comparative analysis demonstrated that this shared conceptual approach provides relatively consistent procedural protection across Canadian jurisdictions while simultaneously obscuring neurodata's distinctive characteristics. Existing legal classifications treat neurodata primarily as informational or health-related data rather than as information capable of revealing cognitive processes, mental states, or personal identity. Consequently, although neurodata benefits from established privacy protections, the legal framework remains oriented towards conventional data protection rather than neurotechnology-specific governance. Neurorights likewise remain absent from Canadian legislation, with equivalent protections arising indirectly through general privacy and health information law.

Collectively, these findings indicate that Canadian neurodata governance is constitutionally decentralised but conceptually harmonised. Despite differences in legislative terminology and institutional responsibility, the federal and provincial frameworks converge around a common understanding of neurodata as a form of protected personal information rather than as a legally exceptional category.

Layer 2. Lawful bases and consent

Comparison across the federal and provincial frameworks demonstrated a high degree of consistency in the legal authority governing neurodata processing. Consent serves as the principal lawful basis across all jurisdictions examined, with federal and provincial legislation requiring meaningful, informed authorisation for the collection, use, and disclosure of personal information, subject to limited statutory exceptions. Unlike the United States, where authorisation varies substantially across regulatory sectors, Canada's governance model remains firmly centred on consent as the primary expression of individual autonomy.

The comparative analysis further showed that Canadian law generally treats consent as a substantive safeguard rather than a procedural formality. Across jurisdictions, consent must be informed, voluntary, and proportionate to the sensitivity of the information involved. Québec and Ontario impose particularly robust requirements for sensitive and health information respectively, while PIPEDA emphasises that individuals must reasonably understand the nature, purpose, and consequences of data processing. Recognition of structural power imbalances, however, remains more developed within healthcare than within employment or consumer settings.

3.

Scientific research is consistently afforded privileged legal treatment throughout the federated framework. Where consent requirements are relaxed, research ethics board approval, confidentiality obligations, de-identification, written agreements, and institutional oversight provide alternative safeguards. Overall, these findings indicate that Canada has developed a highly coherent autonomy-centred governance model in which consent remains the organising principle across both federal and provincial legal systems.

Layer 3. Cross-border transfers

The federated analysis demonstrated that Canada adopts a conditionally permissive approach to cross-border transfers of neurodata. Federal and provincial legislation generally permits international transfers, provided that organisations remain accountable for maintaining appropriate levels of protection throughout the data lifecycle. Rather than imposing broad prohibitions on international transfers, Canadian law relies upon organisational accountability, contractual safeguards, and, in Québec, privacy impact assessments to ensure continuing protection following international disclosure.

The comparative analysis revealed modest variation between jurisdictions. Québec has introduced the most comprehensive transfer framework by requiring formal privacy impact assessments before international disclosure of personal information, whereas PIPEDA relies primarily upon the accountability principle and contractual arrangements. Ontario and British Columbia adopt comparatively flexible approaches that apply general privacy obligations without establishing specialised transfer regimes. Despite these procedural differences, all jurisdictions share a common regulatory philosophy that places responsibility upon organisations rather than restricting international data flows themselves.

Taken together, these findings indicate that Canada's governance framework approaches international transfers through institutional accountability rather than territorial control. Existing mechanisms provide practical safeguards for international data sharing while continuing to regulate neurodata through general privacy principles rather than through dedicated neurodata-specific transfer provisions.

Layer 4. Safeguards and oversight

Comparison across the federal and provincial governance frameworks demonstrated a mature institutional system of oversight supporting neurodata protection. Independent privacy commissioners at both federal and provincial levels, together with research ethics boards and specialised health information regulators, provide multiple layers of procedural accountability throughout the information lifecycle. Individuals generally possess rights of access, correction, and withdrawal of consent, although the practical exercise of these rights varies across jurisdictions.

The comparative analysis further demonstrated that Canadian safeguards are principles-based rather than technologically prescriptive. Organisations are required to implement security measures proportionate to the sensitivity of the information processed, while oversight authorities retain discretion to assess compliance according to the circumstances of each case. This flexible regulatory approach allows governance frameworks to adapt to technological developments but also creates variability in organisational implementation. Oversight remains strongest within healthcare and research contexts, whereas commercial applications rely more heavily upon general privacy obligations.

Overall, these findings indicate that Canada has developed a preventive governance model grounded in institutional accountability and enforceable individual rights. Although oversight mechanisms are well established, they continue to address neurodata primarily through conventional privacy regulation rather than through governance frameworks specifically designed for emerging neurotechnologies.

Layer 5. Enforcement and remedies

The federated analysis demonstrated that Canada possesses well-developed enforcement mechanisms distributed across federal and provincial institutions. Privacy commissioners investigate complaints, conduct compliance reviews, and exercise varying degrees of order-making authority, while judicial remedies and administrative sanctions complement regulatory oversight. Provincial regimes, particularly Québec, provide stronger enforcement powers and more substantial financial penalties than the federal PIPEDA framework, resulting in some variation in regulatory capacity across constitutional levels.

The comparative analysis nevertheless showed considerable consistency in the overall allocation of legal responsibility. Across jurisdictions, primary liability rests with organisations responsible for processing personal information, while individuals may seek redress through administrative complaints and, in many cases, judicial proceedings. Existing enforcement mechanisms effectively support compliance with established privacy obligations but remain focused on traditional data protection harms rather than risks uniquely associated with neurotechnology, such as cognitive profiling, mental inference, or behavioural manipulation.

Collectively, these findings indicate that Canada's enforcement framework provides a credible and institutionally mature foundation for neurodata governance. Provincial variation reflects differences in regulatory design rather than fundamentally different legal philosophies, reinforcing the overall coherence of the federated governance model.

Layer 6. Contractual governance

The comparative analysis identified comparatively limited statutory regulation of contractual governance within Canadian neurodata law. Public legislation establishes the primary legal framework governing the collection, use, and disclosure of neurodata, while contractual arrangements principally serve to implement statutory obligations through research agreements, service provider contracts, institutional collaborations, and data-sharing arrangements. Existing legislation provides relatively little direct regulation of contractual relationships governing downstream uses of neurodata.

As neurotechnology expands beyond traditional healthcare and academic research, contractual governance is likely to assume increasing practical significance. Organisations routinely rely upon contractual mechanisms to allocate responsibility, manage confidentiality, and regulate data sharing, while remaining subject to overarching statutory privacy obligations. Compared with jurisdictions where commercial contractual arrangements play a more autonomous regulatory role, Canadian governance continues to position contracts as instruments implementing public law rather than replacing it.

Taken together, these findings indicate that contractual governance currently occupies a complementary position within Canada's broader legal framework. Public regulation remains the dominant source of legal authority, while private ordering facilitates the practical operation of research, healthcare, and commercial data-sharing arrangements. As neurotechnology continues to evolve, contractual governance is likely to become increasingly important, but within a governance model that remains firmly anchored in statutory privacy law.
