Tiered Neurodata Risk Classification Framework and Neurodata Governance Decision Tool

The comparative analysis found that neurodata were rarely recognised expressly as a distinct legal object and were more commonly governed through categories such as health data, biometric data, sensitive personal information or general personal data. These classifications frequently rely on concepts including identifiability, traceability, sensitivity and processing purpose. The coding did not, however, systematically examine the legal status of derivatives, embeddings, synthetic neurodata, model weights or other post-transformation artefacts. It therefore does not establish that protection necessarily persists, weakens or terminates following technical transformation.

To address this unresolved governance question, we developed the proposed Tiered Neurodata Risk Classification Framework (Supplementary Figure 3). The framework uses functional exposure to describe the capacity of a neurodata object or derivative artefact to support identification, tracing, inference, reconstruction, profiling or other governance-relevant effects. Functional exposure supplements rather than replaces applicable statutory classification. Assignment to a governance tier does not determine whether an artefact constitutes personal, health, biometric or other regulated data under a particular legal system.

Tiers 1-3 build on familiar considerations of aggregation, participant linkage, identifiability and traceability. Tiers 4 and 5 are proposed methodological extensions addressing functionally revealing derivatives and model-associated or computationally persistent artefacts. Technical transformation does not automatically increase or reduce the applicable tier. Similarly, incorporation into an AI model triggers assessment but does not, by itself, establish that the resulting artefact belongs in Tier 5. Tier 5 applies only where there is evidence or reasonable uncertainty that neural information persists within a model or computational infrastructure in a manner capable of creating continuing functional exposure.

The Neurodata Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 6) operationalises the framework through questions concerning the particular object to be stored, analysed, transferred or reused. It supports provisional tier assignment and identifies corresponding baseline safeguards. The assessment considers both technical form and functional exposure; it does not authorise processing, establish the legal status of the object or replace legal, ethics, institutional or repository review. Where relevant information is unavailable, a provisional classification may be applied until the uncertainty has been resolved.

The tool is the first stage of the proposed workflow. A proposed transfer or external access pathway triggers the Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 7). Technical transformation triggers the Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 8). After the relevant assessments have been completed, the MDTAA Clause Selection Tool (Supplementary Table 9) maps their outputs to modules of the Modular Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement. A material change in the object, purpose, recipient, linkage, technical environment or deployment context triggers reassessment at the relevant stage.

Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool

After provisional tier assignment, the Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Neuro-TADT) assesses whether the safeguards associated with that tier can be maintained across a proposed sharing, repository, remote-access, cloud or cross-border pathway (Supplementary Table 7). The tool evaluates the pathway rather than reclassifying the neurodata object.

This component was informed by findings from Layers 3-5. The comparative analysis showed that transfer pathways depend on different combinations of statutory mechanisms, institutional approval, repository governance, technical safeguards, enforcement arrangements and contractual controls. Legal authorisation alone does not determine whether the safeguards required for a particular neurodata object can be implemented in the receiving environment.

The Neuro-TADT considers the recipient and any subprocessors; the mode and location of access; the applicable transfer mechanism and approvals; downloading and retention; linkage; AI-related use; onward sharing; and the receiving environment's capacity to implement the required safeguards. It produces one of four proposed outcomes: proceed subject to applicable approvals; proceed after supplementary safeguards have been implemented; redesign the pathway; or do not proceed and obtain specialist review. These outcomes provide governance decision support and do not constitute findings that a transfer is lawful or unlawful under applicable law. Where the activity involves transformation or model development, the user is directed to the Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool.

Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool

The Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool addresses a post-transformation governance question that was not directly measured through the comparative coding (Supplementary Table 8). It is a normative and methodological extension of the six-layer framework rather than an empirical finding that existing protection necessarily changes after transformation.

The tool is applied when neurodata are transformed into features, embeddings, synthetic data, predictive outputs, trained models or other computational artefacts. It considers the nature of the transformation; whether the artefact can circulate independently; its capacity to support identification, inference, reconstruction or profiling; whether neural information may persist through memorisation or other computational mechanisms; the risk of extraction, inversion or membership inference; and the availability of provenance, access, retention, deletion, decommissioning and, where technically feasible, unlearning controls.

Technical transformation or model incorporation initiates assessment but does not predetermine the outcome. The existing tier may be retained where there is documented evidence that functional exposure has not changed materially. A functionally revealing derivative is referred to the Neurodata Governance Decision Tool for possible Tier 4 classification. A model-associated artefact is considered for Tier 5 only where neural information persists, or may reasonably persist, in a manner creating continuing functional exposure. Unresolved uncertainty requires specialist technical, legal, ethics or institutional review. Where transformation affects an existing transfer or access pathway, the Neuro-TADT must also be repeated.

MDTAA Clause Selection Tool

Layer 6 demonstrated that contractual instruments form an important component of operational governance, particularly where neurodata move between institutions, repositories, service providers or jurisdictions. Existing agreements provide important foundations but may require supplementation where a project involves derivative neurodata, AI processing, computational persistence, specialised access controls or community-governance requirements.

The MDTAA Clause Selection Tool (Supplementary Table 9) is applied after the preceding assessments, where relevant. It maps the provisional tier, transfer conditions, transformation findings and additional institutional or community requirements to the corresponding modules of the Modular Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement. Relevant modules may address cross-border transfer, supplementary safeguards, enhanced neurodata protection, derivatives, AI and model governance, controlled-access infrastructure, onward transfer, dataset linkage, permitted inference, audit, retention, deletion, model unlearning, community governance and benefit-sharing.

The tool does not draft project-specific language, establish enforceability or create a lawful basis for processing or transfer. The completed agreement remains subject to applicable law and any required legal, ethics, repository, institutional or regulatory review. If the neurodata object, transfer pathway, or downstream use changes materially, the applicable assessments and contractual modules must be reconsidered.

Supplementary Figure 3 | Proposed Tiered Neurodata Risk Classification Framework based on functional exposure.

The framework supports provisional classification of a neurodata object according to its capacity to enable identification, tracing, inference, reconstruction, or profiling. Tiers 1-3 build on familiar considerations of aggregation, participant linkage, and traceability. Tiers 4 and 5 are proposed methodological extensions addressing functionally revealing derivatives and model-associated or computationally persistent artefacts. Technical form alone does not determine tier assignment: transformation may retain, diminish or increase functional exposure, and incorporation into an AI model triggers assessment rather than automatic Tier 5 classification. The framework underpins the Neurodata Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 6) and does not determine an artefact's status under applicable law.

Tier terminology.

A candidate tier identifies evidence that may support a particular Risk Tier and requires further assessment; it is not itself a final tier assignment. A provisional tier is a temporary protective classification applied while material uncertainty remains. A confirmed tier is assigned once the relevant assessment has established that the applicable Functional Exposure criteria are met. Where more than one confirmed tier applies, the highest applicable tier governs.

The Neurodata Governance Assessment Record is the project's consolidated record of assessments completed using Supplementary Tables 6-9. It may consist of annotated copies of the applicable tools and linked supporting records. For each applicable step, record the answer, reasons, supporting evidence, outstanding actions, responsible person and date. Identify the assessed object and version, proposed activity, assessment version and reviewer. Where the MDTAA applies, incorporate or reference classification findings in Schedule B, transfer and access findings in Schedule C, and derivative, model and repository governance findings in Schedule D, as applicable. Record module-selection findings with references to the provisions and schedules implementing them. The assessment record may be maintained independently where no MDTAA is used.

Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Neuro-TADT)

After assigning a functional-exposure tier using the Neurodata Governance Decision Tool (NGDT), researchers apply the Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Neuro-TADT) to determine whether a proposed transfer or access pathway has the capacity to implement and maintain the safeguards required for that tier (Supplementary Table 7). The tool applies to physical transfer and to remote access from another legal jurisdiction, including access through repositories, cloud platforms, trusted research environments, federated systems and other external computational infrastructures. It evaluates the proposed pathway rather than reclassifying the neurodata object.

The comparative analysis showed that formal authorisation to transfer or access neurodata does not necessarily ensure continuity of protection after the data enter a different legal, institutional or technical environment. Risks may arise from differences in recipient oversight, access controls, technical infrastructure, enforcement arrangements, onward sharing, dataset linkage, AI-enabled processing and downstream reuse. The Neuro-TADT therefore begins by confirming that the applicable lawful basis, transfer mechanism and required legal, ethical, institutional, repository or regulatory approvals have been identified. These determinations remain governed by applicable law and authorised decision-making bodies; completion of the tool does not establish legal permissibility, adequacy or equivalence.

The Neuro-TADT then examines the proposed activity, access modality, recipient organisation, destination and hosting jurisdictions, receiving governance environment, technical safeguards, intended uses, onward-transfer arrangements and capacity for continuing oversight and accountability. These conditions are assessed against the safeguards required for the tier assigned through the NGDT. The relevant question is not whether the receiving environment is formally "equivalent" to the originating environment, but whether the required safeguards can be implemented, verified and maintained throughout the proposed transfer, access and downstream-use pathway.

The assessment produces one of four outcomes: proceed; proceed after supplementary safeguards are implemented; redesign the transfer or access pathway; or do not proceed. Higher functional exposure generally requires stronger controls over access, reuse, linkage, onward transfer, technical persistence, monitoring and accountability. Where dataset linkage is planned, the NGDT must be reapplied before the linkage occurs to determine whether the anticipated combination changes functional exposure or the assigned tier. The transfer or access pathway must then be reconsidered using the resulting classification.

Where the activity involves technical transformation, derivative generation, synthetic-data generation or AI/model incorporation, the user must also complete the Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 8).

The Neuro-TADT is therefore the second decision point in the sequential governance workflow. The NGDT determines the safeguards provisionally required for the neurodata object or governed artefact; the Neuro-TADT determines whether those safeguards can be maintained across the proposed transfer or access pathway. Its findings subsequently inform the contractual modules selected through the MDTAA Clause Selection Tool (Supplementary Table 9). The assessment must be repeated when a material change occurs, including a change in recipient, jurisdiction, access model, repository, infrastructure, linkage, AI use, onward-sharing arrangement, approved purpose or functional exposure. In this way, the Neuro-TADT supports continuity of protection while remaining complementary to applicable law, ethics review, institutional governance, repository requirements and project-specific legal advice.

Interpretive note: A Neuro-TADT outcome provides structured governance decision support. It does not independently authorise processing, establish formal legal adequacy or replace any required legal, ethics, institutional, repository or regulatory determination.

Outcome Decision Criterion 1 Proceed subject to applicable approvals

Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool

The comparative analysis showed that legal protection for neurodata generally depends on statutory classifications associated with identifiable, health-related, biometric or otherwise sensitive information. The application of those classifications may become less certain after neurodata are transformed into features, embeddings, latent representations, synthetic outputs, predictive artefacts or trained models. The original coding instrument did not directly classify these post-transformation artefacts. Rather, cross-layer analysis identified an unresolved governance question: whether and how protection should continue when a transformed artefact retains the capacity to support neural inference, reconstruction, extraction, profiling or other consequential uses. The Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool represents normative method development informed by this identified uncertainty.

The tool is applied whenever neurodata undergo, or are proposed to undergo, technical transformation, including feature extraction, dimensionality reduction, embedding generation, dataset linkage, predictive modelling, synthetic-data generation, model training, fine-tuning or incorporation into persistent computational infrastructure (Supplementary Table 8). It follows the initial classification undertaken through the Neurodata Governance Decision Tool (NGDT) (Supplementary Table 6). Depending on when transformation occurs within the research workflow, it may be completed before or after the Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Neuro-TADT) (Supplementary Table 7). Where the transformed artefact will be transferred, remotely accessed, hosted, or deployed in another governance environment, the Neuro-TADT must be completed or updated using the outcome of the transformation assessment.

The three tools perform distinct but connected functions. The NGDT assigns the provisional functional-exposure tier and corresponding minimum safeguards for the neurodata object or governed artefact. The Neuro-TADT assesses whether a proposed transfer or access pathway has the capacity to implement and maintain those safeguards. The Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool determines whether technical transformation has altered the functional exposure of the resulting artefact sufficiently to require retention or reassessment of the existing tier. It does not determine the artefact's status under applicable law.

Users assess the particular transformed artefact rather than assuming that it automatically retains the tier of the source neurodata or acquires a higher tier because of its technical form. The assessment considers the nature and purpose of the transformation; the provenance and version of the resulting artefact; whether it can circulate independently; whether participant linkage remains possible; and whether it can support inference, reconstruction, profiling or prediction. It also examines memorisation, extraction, inversion and membership-inference risks; the persistence of neural information within model weights or computational infrastructure; access and deployment conditions; onward use; retention and decommissioning arrangements; and the technical feasibility of deletion or model unlearning. A negative finding concerning participant identification or participant-level inference does not end the assessment, because model persistence, group-level inference or other forms of functional exposure may remain.

The assessment produces five possible outcomes: retain the existing tier; refer for Tier 4 reassessment; refer for Tier 5 reassessment; specialist review required; or do not proceed where the identified exposure cannot be governed. Tier 4 reassessment is indicated where a transformed artefact constitutes functionally revealing derivative neurodata. Tier 5 reassessment is indicated where the artefact constitutes model-associated or computationally persistent neurodata with continuing functional exposure. Model incorporation, synthetic-data generation or storage in an embedding repository does not automatically determine Tier 5 status. Where model incorporation is known but continuing exposure remains uncertain, a provisional classification applies pending completion of the assessment and appropriate specialist review.

Where transformation changes functional exposure, the object is returned to the NGDT for reassessment. Any affected transfer or access pathway must then be reconsidered through the Neuro-TADT. The resulting tier, safeguards, transfer conditions and transformation requirements are subsequently translated into contractual provisions through the MDTAA Clause Selection Tool (Supplementary Table 9). The workflow thereby treats transformation as a governance reassessment point rather than as either the automatic termination or automatic continuation of the source dataset's protections. Tier assignment is informed by functional exposure, while legal status remains determined under applicable law.

MDTAA Clause Selection Tool

The comparative analysis showed that contractual governance frequently performs an important operational role in maintaining protection after neurodata leave their originating research environment (Figures 2f and 4). Statutory authorisation may permit transfer or access, but continuing protection also depends on whether obligations governing permitted use, access, security, onward sharing, oversight and accountability remain effective within the receiving environment. This role becomes particularly important in repositories, cloud platforms, secure computing environments and international collaborations, and where technical transformation creates artefacts whose treatment under existing statutory categories is uncertain.

Existing instruments, including Data Transfer Agreements, Data Use Agreements, repository-access agreements and, where applicable, the European Union Standard Contractual Clauses, provide important foundations for governing confidentiality, security, permitted purposes, party responsibilities and transfer conditions. Nevertheless, conventional agreements may not expressly implement all the safeguards identified through a functional-exposure assessment, particularly those concerning derivative neurodata, dataset linkage, sensitive inference, AI-enabled processing, persistent computational artefacts, model retention, unlearning or community governance. A legally authorised and contractually documented arrangement may therefore remain operationally incomplete if the governance requirements identified through the preceding decision tools are not incorporated into the instruments governing downstream access and use.

The MDTAA Clause Selection Tool translates those governance determinations into the modules of the Modular Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement (MDTAA) (Supplementary Table 9). It is applied after all applicable preceding tools have been completed: the Neurodata Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary

Table 6); the Neurodata Transfer and Access Decision Tool (Neuro-TADT) (Supplementary Table 7) where transfer, external access, remote access or repository use is proposed; and the Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool (Supplementary Table 8) where transformation, derivative generation or AI/model incorporation is involved.

The tool does not establish a lawful basis, approve a transfer, determine legal enforceability or replace project-specific legal, ethical, institutional, repository or regulatory review.

Users progress through a structured sequence of questions addressing the characteristics of the neurodata object or governed artefact, the assigned tier, the proposed transfer or access pathway and the intended downstream activities.

The tool identifies whether the MDTAA requires modules addressing: baseline governance; cross-border transfer; supplementary safeguards; enhanced neurodata protection; derivative neurodata; AI and model governance; controlled-access repositories and infrastructure; onward transfer and subprocessors; prohibition of onward transfer; commercial use and intellectual property; research-only use; dataset linkage; permitted inference and prohibited uses; enhanced audit and monitoring; return, deletion and certification; persistent artefacts, model retention and unlearning; community, collective and Indigenous data governance; benefit sharing and capacity development; project-specific requirements; and contractual coordination and precedence.

Each activated module must record the obligations identified through the preceding assessments, the parties responsible for implementing them and any applicable verification, review or reassessment requirements. The modular structure enables contractual controls to be calibrated to the functional exposure of the particular neurodata object, the proposed activity and the receiving governance environment, rather than applying the same provisions to every arrangement. Selection of a module does not, however, determine an artefact's status under applicable law or establish that the selected provisions will be enforceable in every jurisdiction.

The MDTAA Clause Selection Tool constitutes the contractual implementation stage of the governance workflow. The NGDT identifies the applicable tier and minimum safeguards; the Neuro-TADT assesses whether those safeguards can be implemented and maintained across a proposed transfer or access pathway; and the Derivative and Embedding Governance Decision Tool evaluates whether transformation requires retention or reassessment of the existing tier. The clause-selection tool then maps those determinations to the relevant MDTAA modules. If module selection exposes an unresolved classification, transfer, transformation or safeguard question, the applicable assessment in Supplementary Tables 6-8 must be revisited before the agreement is finalised.

The completed MDTAA complements rather than replaces applicable law, ethics approvals, institutional agreements, repository conditions, Data Use Agreements, Data Transfer Agreements, Standard Contractual Clauses or other mandatory instruments. No transfer, access, transformation or deployment should commence until all required approvals have been obtained and all identified prerequisite safeguards have been implemented. The clause-selection process must also be repeated following a material change in the neurodata object, tier, recipient, jurisdiction, access model, infrastructure, linkage, AI use, onward-sharing arrangement or approved purpose. In this way, contractual implementation remains responsive to changing functional exposure across the data-to-model lifecycle.

Interpretive note: Selection of an MDTAA module does not establish that the underlying processing or transfer is lawful or that the resulting agreement is enforceable in every jurisdiction. 4, Implement and reassess

Do not commence the relevant activity until required approvals and safeguards are in place. Reapply the affected assessments and module-selection steps when material changes alter the object, tier, purpose, recipients, jurisdictions, infrastructure, access arrangements or required safeguards.

PART I -FRAMEWORK AND LEGAL STRUCTURE ARTICLE 1 -TITLE AND NATURE OF AGREEMENT

1.1. This Agreement shall be known as the Modular Neurodata Transfer and Access Agreement ("MDTAA").

1.2.

The MDTAA establishes a modular contractual governance framework for the processing, transfer, access, storage, transformation and reuse of Neurodata and Governed Artefacts.

1.3.

The MDTAA is intended to support conditional interoperability across legally heterogeneous jurisdictions, institutions, repositories and technical environments. It does not purport to harmonise national or regional law or establish formal legal equivalence or adequacy between jurisdictions.

1.4.

The MDTAA is published as a model agreement and governance template. A legally binding agreement arises only when it has been adapted to the relevant project, all applicable Schedules and Annexures have been completed, all required approvals have been obtained, and the agreement has been executed by authorised representatives of the participating Parties.

1.5.

The interpretation and enforceability of the executed MDTAA remain subject to Applicable Law. Nothing in this Agreement determines whether particular Neurodata or a Governed Artefact constitutes Personal Data, health information, biometric data, sensitive information or another legally regulated category.

1.6.

Where equivalent legal or operational roles exist under Applicable Law, the Parties shall interpret references to controllers, processors, joint controllers, repository operators, recipients and related actors by reference to the functions and responsibilities actually exercised.

ARTICLE 2 -DEFINITIONS

For the purposes of this Agreement, unless the context otherwise requires: 2.1. where Clauses, as referred to in Article 3.1., use terms that are defined in Regulation (EU) 2016/679, those terms shall have the same meaning as in that Regulation.

2.2. these Clauses shall be read and interpreted in the light of the provisions of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.2.3. these Clauses shall not be interpreted in a way that conflicts with rights and obligations provided for in Regulation (EU) 2016/679.2.4. "Neurodata" means data derived directly from the measurement, recording or monitoring of human neural activity, structure or function, including EEG, MEG, fMRI, MRI, PET, fNIRS, ECoG, intracranial recordings, implant telemetry and brain-computer-interface signals. Whether information derived through subsequent transformation constitutes Neurodata or another legally regulated category remains determined under Applicable Law and, for contractual governance purposes, through the assessment procedures established by this Agreement. 2.5. "Personal Data" means any information relating to an identified or identifiable natural person as defined under applicable law. 2.6. "Biometric Data" means data resulting from specific technical processing relating to physical, physiological, or behavioural characteristics enabling unique identification. 2.7. "Genetic Data" means personal data relating to inherited or acquired genetic characteristics providing unique information about physiology or health 2.8. "Data Exporter" means the Party transferring data to another Party under this Agreement. 2.9. "Data Importer" means the receiving Party agreeing to process such data in accordance with this Agreement. 2.10. "Data Subject" means an individual to whom the data relate. 2.11. "Functional Exposure" means the capacity of Neurodata or a Governed Artefact to enable identification or tracing, inference, reconstruction, extraction, profiling, prediction, classification, linkage, memorisation or another consequential use concerning an individual or group, irrespective of the artefact's technical form, degree of transformation or removal of direct identifiers. 2.12. "Processing" means any operation performed upon data, whether automated or otherwise. 2.13. "Research Project" means a defined scientific study involving neurodata collection, analysis, or sharing. 2.14. "Controller" and "Processor" shall bear the meanings assigned under the General Data Protection Regulation (EU) 2016/679 ("GDPR") and analogous statutes. 2.15. "Cross-border Transfer" means any communication or remote access of data from one jurisdiction to another. 2.16. "Ethics Oversight Body" means an Institutional Review Board (IRB), Research Ethics Committee (REC), or equivalent authority responsible for ethical assessment. 2.17. "Dynamic Consent" means a digital and ongoing consent mechanism permitting participants to modify sharing preferences over time. 2.18. "Data Steward" means an appointed person ensuring compliance with governance obligations and acting as liaison with data subjects. 2.19. "Anonymisation" means processing intended to prevent information from being attributed to an identified or identifiable person using means reasonably likely to be available in the relevant context. Whether information is legally anonymised shall be determined under Applicable Law. Description of an object as anonymised, de-identified, aggregated or synthetic does not, by itself, determine its functional-exposure tier under this Agreement. 2.20. "Pseudonymisation" means processing in which identifiers are replaced by codes enabling re-identification only under controlled conditions. 2.21. "Applicable Law" means all statutory, regulatory, and ethical norms governing data protection, research conduct, and cross-border transfers within relevant jurisdictions. 2.22. "Derivative Neurodata" means a feature, metric, representation, annotation, label, prediction, profile, reconstruction, statistical output, synthetic output or other artefact produced from, inferred from or generated using Neurodata. Derivative Neurodata may include spectral decompositions, connectivity measures, feature vectors, latent representations, embeddings, classifications and predictive outputs. Derivative status alone does not determine the applicable Risk Tier or the artefact's status under Applicable Law. 2.23. "Embeddings" means vector representations, latent encodings, compressed representations, or internal model states generated by AI or machine-learning systems that are trained on or exposed to Neurodata. This includes: (a) latent vectors derived from deep learning models or neural networks; (b) feature embeddings used for classification, clustering, or prediction; (c) intermediate representations produced during model training; 3.

(d) neural manifolds or dimensionality-reduced spaces derived from Neurodata; (e) any representation that captures structure, pattern, or identifiable characteristics of individual neural activity.

Embeddings constitute illustrative artefacts requiring assessment under Annexures 1 and 3. Their generation, storage or incorporation into a computational system does not automatically establish Tier 4 or Tier 5 status. The applicable tier shall be informed by the Functional Exposure of the specific embedding under assessment.

2.24.

"High-Risk Neurodata" means any category of Neurodata or Neural Derivative Data that, due to its sensitivity, identifiability, interpretability, or potential misuse, requires enhanced protections. High-Risk Neurodata includes: (a) raw neural signals (EEG, MEG, fNIRS, ECoG, sEEG, LFP, spike trains); (b) data captured from implanted or semi-invasive neural devices; (c) brain-computer interface (BCI) input/output logs; (d) neural activity capable of revealing cognitive, emotional, or mental state information; (e) data used to infer clinical conditions, neurological disorders, or behavioural traits; (f) neuroimaging data (MRI, fMRI, DTI, PET) where individual identification is possible; (g) embeddings or latent representations that allow reconstruction, inference, or profiling; (h) neural signatures known to be unique or quasi-unique to individuals; (i) any neurodata collected from vulnerable populations, including: • minors, • cognitively impaired participants, • Indigenous or community-governed groups, or • historically marginalised populations.

2.25. "Governed Artefact"means Neurodata, Derivative Neurodata, an embedding, synthetic output, model-associated artefact, computational representation or other object specified in Schedules A or B that either retains Functional Exposure or is made subject to contractual governance under this Agreement. Classification as a Governed Artefact does not determine the object's legal status under Applicable Law. 2.26. "Neuro-TADT" means the assessment of a proposed transfer or access pathway conducted under Annexure 2 and recorded in Schedule C. 2.27. "Repository" means any data platform, archive, database, federated infrastructure, cloud-hosted environment, trusted research environment, or other system used to store, manage, disseminate, provide access to, or govern Neurodata or Governed Artefacts. 2.28. "Data Access Committee (DAC)" means a body responsible for reviewing, approving, monitoring, or restricting access to Neurodata, Governed Artefacts, or related research outputs. 2.29. "Repository Operator" means the institution, organisation, or entity responsible for administering a Repository and enforcing applicable governance requirements." 2.30. "Continuity of Protection" means the preservation of applicable governance obligations and safeguards as Neurodata or a Governed Artefact moves across jurisdictions, institutions, repositories, technical environments, derivative forms and downstream computational uses. 2.31. "Risk Tier" means the functional-exposure governance classification assigned under Annexure 1. The classification may be provisional while required evidence or review remains outstanding, or confirmed when the applicable assessment is complete. A Risk Tier does not determine statutory status under Applicable Law. 2.32. "Required Safeguards" means the legal, ethical, institutional, repository, technical and contractual measures identified as necessary for the applicable Risk Tier and proposed activity. 2.33. "Remote Access" means access to Neurodata or a Governed Artefact from a legal jurisdiction, institution or governance environment other than the environment in which the object is hosted, whether or not a downloadable copy is created. 2.34. "Material Change" means a change in the Neurodata object, Governed Artefact, recipient, jurisdiction, purpose, access model, repository, infrastructure, dataset linkage, transformation, AI use, onward-sharing arrangement or other circumstance capable of altering Functional Exposure or the Required Safeguards.

ARTICLE 3 -PURPOSE AND OBJECTIVES

ARTICLE 3 -PURPOSE AND OBJECTIVES (a) The purpose of these Clauses is to ensure compliance with the requirements of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 of the European Parliament and of the Council of 27 April 2016 on the protection of natural persons with regard to the processing of personal data and on the free movement of such data (General Data Protection Regulation) for the transfer of personal data to a third country.

3.1. Purpose and Scope (GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses Requirement)

(b) The Parties: (i) the natural or legal person(s), public authority/ies, agency/ies or other body/ies transferring the personal data, as listed in Schedule A (each hereinafter a "Data Exporter"), and (ii) the entity/ies in a third country receiving the personal data from the Data Exporter, directly or indirectly via another entity also Party to these Clauses, as listed in Schedule A (each hereinafter a "Data Importer"), have agreed to these Standard Contractual Clauses ("Clauses").

(c) These Clauses apply with respect to the transfer of personal data as specified in Schedule B.

(d) The details of the transfer(s), and in particular the categories of personal data that are transferred and the purpose(s) for which they are transferred, are specified in Schedule B.

3.

(e) The Appendix to these Clauses containing the Annexes referred to therein forms an integral part of these Clauses.

3.2. Objectives of the Model Data Transfer Agreement (MDTA)

In addition to the requirements set out in Clause 3.1, the objectives of this Agreement are to: (a) facilitate the lawful and ethical sharing of neurodata and related health, biometric, and genetic data for scientific research, innovation, and public benefit; (b) support conditional interoperability across divergent legal and institutional environments through a modular governance framework, without requiring or asserting global legal harmonisation; (c) ensure the protection of fundamental rights, including mental privacy, autonomy, dignity, non-discrimination, and cognitive liberty; (d) promote transparency, accountability, and equitable benefit sharing across jurisdictions and research partnerships; and (e) support interoperability with digital governance infrastructures, including but not limited to the ezGov platform, for automated compliance and contract generation.

(f) facilitate conditional interoperability across legally heterogeneous jurisdictions by preserving continuity of protection without requiring full legal harmonisation.

3.3. Relationship Between MDTA Objectives and GDPR SCC Compliance

The Parties acknowledge that: (a) compliance with these Clauses does not exempt them from any mandatory national or regional legal obligations; (b) the MDTA supplements but does not replace the obligations imposed by the GDPR, the SCCs, or other applicable data protection laws; and (c) where conflict arises, the SCC obligations prevail to ensure that an essentially equivalent level of protection is maintained for personal data transferred to third countries.

ARTICLE 3A -COMMUNITY BENEFIT, EQUITY, AND RESPONSIBLE USE

3A.1. Commitment to Community Benefit

The Parties acknowledge that neurodata, particularly originating from historically marginalised or under-resourced populations, requires a governance framework grounded in fairness, reciprocity, and equitable benefit-sharing.

3A.2. Equitable Research Practices

The Data Importer shall ensure that: (a) scientific outputs include appropriate attribution and representation of source communities;

3A.5. Transparency and Return of Results

Where appropriate, and in accordance with ethics approvals, results shall be communicated back to communities in accessible formats that avoid therapeutic misconception or stigmatisation.

3A.6. Review and Monitoring

The Data Exporter may require periodic reviews of the community impact of the research or data use.

ARTICLE 3B -INTERPRETATION OF SCC ANNEXURES AND MDTAA ANNEXURES

References to Annex I, Annex II and Annex III in the European Union Standard Contractual Clauses refer exclusively to the official SCC Appendix adopted under Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. They shall not be interpreted as references to Annexures 1-5 of the MDTAA.

ARTICLE 4 -SCOPE OF APPLICATION

4.1. Contractual scope

The MDTAA applies to the Neurodata and Governed Artefacts identified in Schedules A and B and to the processing, transfer, Remote Access, repository deposit, storage, transformation, reuse and downstream activities specified by the Parties.

4.2. Activities covered

The MDTAA may govern:

4.3. Relationship to legal classification

The inclusion of an object within the contractual scope of the MDTAA does not determine whether it constitutes Personal Data, health information, biometric data, sensitive information or another legally regulated category. Its legal status remains determined under Applicable Law.

4.4. Anonymised and transformed information

Information shall not be excluded automatically from this Agreement merely because it has been described as anonymised, de-identified, aggregated, synthetic or technically transformed. Where the Parties elect to govern the information contractually, or where continuing Functional Exposure is identified, the applicable provisions of this Agreement shall continue to apply.

4.5. Domestic and cross-border arrangements

The MDTAA may be used for domestic, cross-institutional or international arrangements. The Neuro-TADT shall be completed whenever the circumstances specified in Article 13A and Annexure 2 apply.

4.6. Application of the SCCs

The SCCs apply only where the relevant transfer falls within their legal scope and the appropriate SCC Module has been selected. The remaining provisions of the MDTAA may apply independently of the SCCs where the Parties use the MDTAA for another legally authorised arrangement.

4.7. Mandatory law

Nothing in this Agreement authorises processing, access, sharing, transfer or reuse prohibited by Applicable Law or displaces any mandatory consent, ethics, regulatory, institutional, repository or data-sovereignty requirement.

ARTICLE 5 -RELATIONSHIP BETWEEN PARTIES

5.1. Designation of Roles

Each Party's role shall be determined for the relevant processing operation by reference to its actual functions and Applicable Law. Exporter or importer status does not itself determine whether a Party is a Controller or Processor. For GDPR purposes, a Controller determines the purposes and essential means of processing; Joint Controllers determine them jointly; and a Processor processes Personal Data on behalf of a Controller. Schedule A shall identify each Party and summarise its role or roles. Schedule B, Part F.3, shall record the operation-specific assessment, including its factual basis and any Controller on whose behalf a Processor acts. A Party may hold different roles for different operations. Unresolved role classifications shall be referred for institutional data-protection or legal review before the affected processing or transfer begins.

Articles 5.2-5.5 apply only where the SCCs fall within their legal scope and the corresponding Module is selected for the identified transfer in Schedule A, Part E.5.

5.2. Application of SCC Module 1 (Controller → Controller Transfers)

Where both the Data Exporter and Data Importer act as Controllers, the obligations in Module 1 of the GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses shall apply in full. Each Controller shall act consistently with its documented role, including any joint-controller arrangement under Article 5.6, and each shall comply with its respective data protection obligations, including transparency, lawful basis, data minimisation, accuracy, integrity, confidentiality, and data subject rights.

5.3. Application of SCC Module 2 (Controller → Processor Transfers)

Where the Data Exporter acts as a Controller and the Data Importer acts as a Processor, the Parties agree that Module 2 of the GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses shall apply.

3.

The Processor shall implement all technical, organisational, and security measures required under Article 6, the applicable Risk Tier, Schedule D and Annexure 5.

5.4. Application of SCC Module 3 (Processor → Processor Transfers).

Where the Data Exporter and Data Importer act as Processors, the Parties agree that Module 3 of the GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses shall apply.

The receiving Processor must: (a) act only on instructions from the Controller communicated through the exporting Processor; (b) ensure equivalent obligations to those imposed on the exporting Processor; (c) maintain all security measures required under Article 6, the applicable Risk Tier, Schedule D and Annexure 5; and (d) return or delete personal data at the instruction of the Controller or the exporting Processor.

5.5. Application of SCC Module 4 (Processor → Controller Transfers).

Where the Data Exporter is a Processor and the Data Importer is a Controller, the Parties agree that Module 4 of the GDPR Standard Contractual Clauses shall apply.

The Data Importer (Controller) shall: (a) ensure a lawful basis for further processing under Articles 6 and 9 GDPR; (b) provide all necessary information to Data Subjects, unless such responsibility has been contractually delegated; (c) comply with all data protection principles under Article 6 of this Agreement; and (d) notify the exporting Processor of any instructions inconsistent with the SCCs or applicable law.

5.6. Joint Controller Arrangements.

Where the Parties act as Joint Controllers, their respective responsibilities shall be set out in Schedule A, consistent with Article 26 GDPR. Unless otherwise agreed, Joint Controllers are jointly responsible for ensuring: (a) transparency to Data Subjects; (b) compliance with data subject rights; and (c) implementation of the technical, organisational, and security measures required under Article 6, the applicable Risk Tier, Schedule D and Annexure 5.

5.7. Consistency with SCC Obligations.

In the event of conflict between this Article and the provisions of the SCCs, the Standard Contractual Clauses prevail, in line with Article 3.3 of this Agreement, to ensure an essentially equivalent level of protection for transferred personal data.

(e) complete all governing-law, forum, supervisory-authority and other mandatory fields; and (f) ensure consistency between the SCC Appendix and Schedules A-D of the MDTAA.

5B.3.

The SCCs shall not be modified except as permitted by Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914. Additional MDTAA protections shall operate as supplementary contractual obligations and shall not contradict the SCCs or prejudice the rights and freedoms of data subjects.

5B.4.

In the event of an irreconcilable conflict concerning a transfer governed by the SCCs, the SCCs shall prevail to the extent required by Applicable Law.

5B.5.

Where the SCCs do not apply, no reference to them in this Agreement shall be interpreted as establishing legal adequacy, equivalence or authority for the proposed transfer.

5B.6. Decision-Support Assistance with SCC Completion

Where Decision (EU) 2021/914 applies, the MDTAA decision-support process may assist the Parties to compile the information required to complete the applicable SCC Appendix from Schedules A-D and other approved project records. This assistance may include preparation of draft information for SCC Annex I.A, Annex I.B, Annex I.C, Annex II and, where applicable, Annex III. The decision-support process shall not alter the official SCC text, conclusively determine a Party's legal role, select a competent supervisory authority without an adequate legal basis, or independently establish that a transfer is lawful. Any unresolved role classification, SCC applicability question, Module selection or mandatory SCC field shall be referred for appropriate institutional data protection or legal review before execution.

ARTICLE 6 -GOVERNING PRINCIPLES

6.1.

General Data Protection Principles.

The Parties shall comply with all applicable data protection principles under this Agreement, including lawfulness, fairness, transparency, purpose limitation, data minimisation, accuracy, storage limitation, integrity, confidentiality, accountability, and all additional principles applicable to neurodata and health-related data as set out in this Agreement.

6.2. Integration of the EU Standard Contractual Clauses (SCCs) -Clause 8

In accordance with Articles 3 and 5 of this Agreement, and for any transfer of Personal Data to a third country, the Parties hereby incorporate Clause 8 (Data Protection Safeguards) of the European Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021, including all Module-specific provisions (Modules 1-4), verbatim and without modification, as follows: 3.

Clause 8 (Data Protection Safeguards) of the European Commission Implementing Decision (EU) 2021/914 of 4 June 2021

(a) Each Party shall ensure that the personal data is accurate and, where necessary, kept up to date. The data importer shall take every reasonable step to ensure that personal data that is inaccurate, having regard to the purpose(s) of processing, is erased or rectified without delay.

(b) If one of the Parties becomes aware that the personal data it has transferred or received is inaccurate, or has become outdated, it shall inform the other Party without undue delay.

(c) The data importer shall ensure that the personal data is adequate, relevant and limited to what is necessary in relation to the purpose(s) of processing.

8.4. Storage Limitation

The data importer shall retain the personal data for no longer than necessary for the purpose(s) for which it is processed. It shall put in place appropriate technical or organisational measures to ensure compliance with this obligation, including erasure or anonymisation of the data and all back-ups at the end of the retention period. 8.5.

Security of Processing (a)

The data importer and, during transmission, also the data exporter shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of the personal data, including protection against a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access (hereinafter 'personal data breach'). In assessing the appropriate level of security, they shall take due account of the state of the art, the costs of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purpose(s) of processing and the risks involved in the processing for the data subject. The Parties shall in particular consider having recourse to encryption or pseudonymisation, including during transmission, where the purpose of processing can be fulfilled in that manner.

(b) The Parties have agreed on the technical and organisational measures set out in Annex II. The data importer shall carry out regular checks to ensure that these measures continue to provide an appropriate level of security.

(c) The data importer shall ensure that persons authorised to process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality.

(d) In the event of a personal data breach concerning personal data processed by the data importer under these Clauses, the data importer shall take appropriate measures to address the personal data breach, including measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects.

(e) In case of a personal data breach that is likely to result in a risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the data importer shall without undue delay notify both the data exporter and the competent supervisory authority pursuant to Clause 13. Such notification shall contain i) a description of the nature of the breach (including, where possible, categories and approximate number of data subjects and personal data records concerned), ii) its likely consequences, iii) the measures taken or proposed to address the breach, and iv) the details of a contact point from whom more information can be obtained. To the extent it is not possible for the data importer to provide all the information at the same time, it may do so in phases without undue further delay.

(f) In case of a personal data breach that is likely to result in a high risk to the rights and freedoms of natural persons, the data importer shall also notify without undue delay the data subjects concerned of the personal data breach and its nature, if necessary in cooperation with the data exporter, together with the information referred to in paragraph (e), points ii) to iv), unless the data importer has implemented measures to significantly reduce the risk to the rights or freedoms of natural persons, or notification would involve disproportionate efforts. In the latter case, the data importer shall instead issue a public communication or take a similar measure to inform the public of the personal data breach.

(g) The data importer shall document all relevant facts relating to the personal data breach, including its effects and any remedial action taken, and keep a record thereof.

8.6. Sensitive Data

Where the transfer involves personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, genetic data, or biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or a person's sex life or sexual orientation, or data relating to criminal convictions or offences (hereinafter 'sensitive data'), the data importer shall apply specific restrictions and/or additional safeguards adapted to the specific nature of the data and the risks involved. This may include restricting the personnel permitted to access the personal data, additional security measures (such as pseudonymisation) and/or additional restrictions with respect to further disclosure. This requires rendering the data anonymous in such a way that the individual is no longer identifiable by anyone, in line with recital 26 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679, and that this process is irreversible. 8.7.

Onward Transfers

The data importer shall not disclose the personal data to a third party located outside the European Union (in the same country as the data importer or in another third country, hereinafter ('onward transfer') unless the third party is or agrees to be bound by these Clauses, under the appropriate Module. Otherwise, an onward transfer by the data importer may only take place if: (i) it is to a country benefitting from an adequacy decision pursuant to Article 45 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 that covers the onward transfer; (ii) the third party otherwise ensures appropriate safeguards pursuant to Articles 46 or 47 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 with respect to the processing in question; (iii) the third party enters into a binding instrument with the data importer ensuring the same level of data protection as under these Clauses, and the data importer provides a copy of these safeguards to the data exporter; (iv) it is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims in the context of specific administrative, regulatory or judicial proceedings; (v) it is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person; (vi) where none of the other conditions apply, the data importer has obtained the explicit consent of the data subject for an onward transfer in a specific situation, after having informed him/her of its purpose(s), the identity of the recipient and the possible risks of such transfer to him/her due to the lack of appropriate data protection safeguards.

In this case, the data importer shall inform the data exporter and, at the request of the latter, shall transmit to it a copy of the information provided to the data subject.

Any onward transfer is subject to compliance by the data importer with all the other safeguards under these Clauses, in particular purpose limitation.

8.8. Processing under the Authority of the Data Importer

The data importer shall ensure that any person acting under its authority, including a processor, processes the data only on its instructions.

8.9. Documentation and Compliance (a) Each Party shall be able to demonstrate compliance with its obligations under these Clauses. In particular, the data importer shall keep appropriate documentation of the processing activities carried out under its responsibility.

(b) The data importer shall make such documentation available to the competent supervisory authority on request.

MODULE TWO: Transfer controller to processor

MODULE TWO: Transfer controller to processor 3.

8.1. Instructions

(a) The data importer shall process the personal data only on documented instructions from the data exporter. The data exporter may give such instructions throughout the duration of the contract.

(b) The data importer shall immediately inform the data exporter if it is unable to follow those instructions.

8.2. Purpose Limitation

The data importer shall process the personal data only for the specific purpose(s) of the transfer, as set out in Schedule B, unless on further instructions from the data exporter.

8.3. Transparency

On request, the data exporter shall make a copy of these Clauses, including the Append I as completed by the Parties, available to the data subject free of charge. To the extent necessary to protect business secrets or other confidential information, including the measures described in Annex II and personal data, the data exporter may redact part of the text of the Appendix to these Clauses prior to sharing a copy, but shall provide a meaningful summary where the data subject would otherwise not be able to understand its content or exercise his/her rights. On request, the Parties shall provide the data subject with the reasons for the redactions, to the extent possible without revealing the redacted information. This Clause is without prejudice to the obligations of the data exporter under Articles 13 and 14 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679.

8.4. Accuracy

If the data importer becomes aware that the personal data it has received is inaccurate, or has become outdated, it shall inform the data exporter without undue delay. In this case, the data importer shall cooperate with the data exporter to erase or rectify the data.

8.5. Duration of processing and erasure or return of data

Processing by the data importer shall only take place for the duration specified in Schedule B. After the end of the provision of the processing services, the data importer shall, at the choice of the data exporter, delete all personal data processed on behalf of the data exporter and certify to the data exporter that it has done so, or return to the data exporter all personal data processed on its behalf and delete existing copies. Until the data is deleted or returned, the data importer shall continue to ensure compliance with these Clauses. In case of local laws applicable to the data importer that prohibit return or deletion of the personal data, the data importer warrants that it will continue to ensure compliance with these Clauses and will only process it to the extent and for as long as required under that local law. This is without prejudice to Clause 14, in particular the requirement for the data importer under Clause 14(e) to notify the data exporter throughout the duration of the contract if it has reason to believe that it is or has become subject to laws or practices not in line with the requirements under Clause 14(a).

8.6. Security of processing (a)

The data importer and, during transmission, also the data exporter shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of the data, including protection against a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access to that data (hereinafter 'personal data breach'). In assessing the appropriate level of security, the Parties shall take due account of the state of the art, the costs of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purpose(s) of processing and the risks involved in the processing for the data subjects. The Parties shall in particular consider having recourse to encryption or pseudonymisation, including during transmission, where the purpose of processing can be fulfilled in that manner. In case of pseudonymisation, the additional information for attributing the personal data to a specific data subject shall, where possible, remain under the exclusive control of the data exporter. In complying with its obligations under this paragraph, the data importer shall at least implement the technical and organisational measures specified in Annex II. The data importer shall carry out regular checks to ensure that these measures continue to provide an appropriate level of security.

3.

(b) The data importer shall grant access to the personal data to members of its personnel only to the extent strictly necessary for the implementation, management and monitoring of the contract. It shall ensure that persons authorised to process the personal data have committed themselves to confidentiality or are under an appropriate statutory obligation of confidentiality.

(c) In the event of a personal data breach concerning personal data processed by the data importer under these Clauses, the data importer shall take appropriate measures to address the breach, including measures to mitigate its adverse effects. The data importer shall also notify the data exporter without undue delay after having become aware of the breach. Such notification shall contain the details of a contact point where more information can be obtained, a description of the nature of the breach (including, where possible, categories and approximate number of data subjects and personal data records concerned), its likely consequences and the measures taken or proposed to address the breach including, where appropriate, measures to mitigate its possible adverse effects. Where, and in so far as, it is not possible to provide all information at the same time, the initial notification shall contain the information then available and further information shall, as it becomes available, subsequently be provided without undue delay.

(d) The data importer shall cooperate with and assist the data exporter to enable the data exporter to comply with its obligations under Regulation (EU) 2016/679, in particular to notify the competent supervisory authority and the affected data subjects, considering the nature of processing and the information available to the data importer.

8.7. Sensitive data

Where the transfer involves personal data revealing racial or ethnic origin, political opinions, religious or philosophical beliefs, or trade union membership, genetic data, or biometric data for the purpose of uniquely identifying a natural person, data concerning health or a person's sex life or sexual orientation, or data relating to criminal convictions and offences (hereinafter 'sensitive data'), the data importer shall apply the specific restrictions and/or additional safeguards described in Schedule B.

8.8. Onward transfers

The data importer shall only disclose the personal data to a third party on documented instructions from the data exporter. In addition, the data may only be disclosed to a third party located outside the European Union (in the same country as the data importer or in another third country, hereinafter 'onward transfer') if the third party is or agrees to be bound by these Clauses, under the appropriate Module, or if: (i) the onward transfer is to a country benefitting from an adequacy decision pursuant to Article 45 of Regulation (EU) 2016/679 that covers the onward transfer; (ii) the third party otherwise ensures appropriate safeguards pursuant to Articles 46 or 47 Regulation of (EU) 2016/679 with respect to the processing in question; (iii) the onward transfer is necessary for the establishment, exercise or defence of legal claims in the context of specific administrative, regulatory or judicial proceedings; (iv) the onward transfer is necessary in order to protect the vital interests of the data subject or of another natural person.

Any onward transfer is subject to compliance by the data importer with all the other safeguards under these Clauses, in particular purpose limitation.

8.9. Documentation and compliance (a)

The data importer shall promptly and adequately deal with enquiries from the data exporter that relate to the processing under these Clauses.

If the data importer becomes aware that the personal data it has received is inaccurate, or has become outdated, it shall inform the data exporter without undue delay. In this case, the data importer shall cooperate with the data exporter to rectify or erase the data.

8.5. Duration of processing and erasure or return of data

Processing by the data importer shall only take place for the duration specified in Schedule B. After the end of the provision of the processing services, the data importer shall, at the choice of the data exporter, delete all personal data processed on behalf of the controller and certify to the data exporter that it has done so, or return to the data exporter all personal data processed on its behalf and delete existing copies. Until the data is deleted or returned, the data importer shall continue to ensure compliance with these Clauses. In case of local laws applicable to the data importer that prohibit return or deletion of the personal data, the data importer warrants that it will continue to ensure compliance with these Clauses and will only process it to the extent and for as long as required under that local law. This is without prejudice to Clause 14, in particular the requirement for the data importer under Clause 14(e) to notify the data exporter throughout the duration of the contract if it has reason to believe that it is or has become subject to laws or practices not in line with the requirements under Clause 14(a). 8.6. Security of processing (a)

The data importer and, during transmission, also the data exporter shall implement appropriate technical and organisational measures to ensure the security of the data, including protection against a breach of security leading to accidental or unlawful destruction, loss, alteration, unauthorised disclosure or access to that data (hereinafter 'personal data breach'). In assessing the appropriate level of security, they shall take due account of the state of the art, the costs of implementation, the nature, scope, context and purpose(s) of processing and the risks involved in the processing for the data subject. The Parties shall in particular consider having recourse to encryption or pseudonymisation, including during transmission, where the purpose of processing can be fulfilled in that manner. In case of pseudonymisation, the additional information for attributing the personal data to a specific data subject shall, where possible, remain under the exclusive control of the data exporter or the controller. In complying with its obligations under this paragraph, the data importer shall at least implement the technical and organisational measures specified in Annex II. The data importer shall carry out regular checks to ensure that these measures continue to provide an appropriate level of security.

(b) The data importer shall grant access to the data to members of its personnel only to the extent strictly necessary for the implementation, management and monitoring of the contract.
